A rattle is fundamentally about a rapid, repeated series of short, sharp knocking sounds — the kind made when hard objects hit each other again and again in quick succession. Almost every meaning of this word either is that sound or describes something that makes that sound.

The most direct meaning of "rattle" is simply the sound — a quick, repeating, hard-knocking noise.

This is not a single knock. It is many small knocks happening one right after the other, creating a continuous clatter. Think of:

  • Someone shaking a tin can filled with small pebbles
  • Hailstones hitting a metal roof
  • Keys being jangled
  • Chains dragging across a stone floor
  • Windows shaking in a strong wind
  • Dishes clattering against each other in a sink

All of these make a "rattle."

In sentences:

  • "We heard a rattle coming from under the car."
  • "The rattle of the train on old tracks lulled him to sleep."
  • "There's a strange rattle in the pipes."
  • "The rattle of gunfire echoed through the city."

Notice something important in the first example: when someone says "there's a rattle in the engine," they mean an unwanted, repeated knocking sound — probably from a loose part. A mechanic will try to "find and fix the rattle." Here, "rattle" refers to both the sound and the problem causing it.
Meaning 2: A Physical Object That Makes This Sound

"Rattle" is also the name for any object made to produce a rattling sound. There are several important types.

The Baby's Rattle

This is the most universally familiar type. A baby's rattle is a small toy, usually with a handle at one end (so an infant can grip it) and a sealed rounded container at the other. Inside that container are small beads, pellets, or seeds. When the baby shakes it, those objects knock rapidly against the walls of the container, creating a cheerful rattling sound.

Babies are naturally drawn to the sound — it stimulates them. The rattle is typically one of the very first toys given to a newborn. Because of this, the word "rattle" and the image of a baby's toy are deeply linked in most people's minds.

The Sports or Stadium Rattle

This type of rattle is a mechanical device — typically a flat board or paddle, mounted on a handle, with a notched gear or cog mechanism. When you swing it around rapidly, the board repeatedly hits the teeth of the gear, producing a loud, sharp rattling clatter.

These were historically very popular among football (soccer) supporters in Britain and Europe. Fans would swing them in the stadium to make noise and support their team. You may still see similar devices at sporting events around the world today.

Musical and Ceremonial Rattles

Across many cultures and throughout history, rattles have been used as percussion instruments and in ceremonies and rituals. Indigenous peoples across the Americas, Africa, and other parts of the world have long used rattles made from gourds, turtle shells, animal hides, and other materials — filled with seeds or pebbles — in music, dance, and spiritual practice.

In an orchestra or band context, a rattle (also called a whip or ratchet depending on the design) can be used for dramatic percussive effects.
Meaning 3: The Rattle of a Rattlesnake

This is one of the most specific and interesting uses. A rattlesnake has a specialized organ at the very tip of its tail — and this organ is called the rattle.

Here is what it looks like and how it works: The rattle is a series of dry, hollow, loosely linked segments made of keratin (the same tough protein that makes up your fingernails). These segments are nested and interlocked, somewhat like a chain of loose rings or beads.

When the snake feels threatened, it vibrates its tail at extremely high speed. The hollow segments knock against each other rapidly, producing the famous buzzing, rattling warning sound. This is the snake's way of saying: I am here. Back away.

Each time a rattlesnake sheds its skin — which happens multiple times each year — a new segment is added to the rattle. Older snakes therefore tend to have longer rattles, though segments can also break off over time.

In sentences:

  • "We heard the rattle before we even saw the snake."
  • "The snake shook its rattle as a warning."

This is a specific and well-known compound noun: the death rattle. It refers to the harsh, gurgling, or rattling sound that sometimes comes from the throat or chest of a person who is in the very final moments of life.

Here is what causes it: As a person approaches death, the muscles in the throat and airways relax completely. Saliva, mucus, or other fluid may gather in the throat and upper airway. When air passes through this accumulated fluid during breathing, it creates a distinctive wet, rattling, or gurgling sound.

Medical professionals and caregivers recognize the death rattle as a sign that death is imminent. It is worth knowing that the dying person is typically not in distress when this happens — the sound is disturbing to those present, but the person making it is usually unconscious or deeply unresponsive.

The Figurative Use of "Death Rattle"

Because of its powerful association with final moments, "death rattle" is commonly used as a figure of speech to describe the last failing stage of something that is coming to an end — a company, a movement, an era, an idea:

  • "The closure of the last remaining factories was the death rattle of the region's industrial age."
  • "The protest was little more than the death rattle of a failing political movement."

Nothing is literally dying in these sentences — the phrase simply captures the idea of something in its very last, terminal phase before it disappears completely.
Meaning 5: A Rattle in a Plant (Botanical Use)

Less commonly known: "rattle" is also the common name for certain wild flowering plants — most notably yellow rattle (Rhinanthus minor) and red rattle. These plants get their name because, when the plant dries out, the seeds inside the seed pods become loose and rattle audibly when the plant is shaken or blown by the wind. Farmers in earlier centuries could hear a field of yellow rattle rustling and rattling in the breeze, which is how the name stuck.

This is a more specialized meaning, but worth knowing because it shows just how consistently the word is tied to that core idea of a rattling sound.
An Older, Now Rare Meaning: Lively Chatter

In older English — particularly 18th- and 19th-century literature — "a rattle" could also refer to a stream of rapid, lively, often shallow or empty talk. The idea was that words were tumbling out quickly, one after another, like the sound of a rattle.

  • "She kept up a cheerful rattle throughout the entire journey."

Occasionally, a person who talked a great deal in this way would themselves be called "a rattle."

This sense is largely old-fashioned and rarely used in everyday modern English, but you will encounter it if you read classic novels — especially English fiction from the 1700s and 1800s (Jane Austen's characters, for instance, sometimes describe each other this way).
The One Thread That Connects Everything

Look back at all six meanings. A baby's toy. A snake's tail. A dying person's final sound. A noise in your car. A flowering plant. A person who talks too much. At first glance, they seem completely unrelated — but they are all connected by exactly one idea:

The rapid, repeated, hard-knocking sound of things hitting each other in quick succession.

Every time you see "rattle" as a noun, ask yourself one simple question: Is this the sound itself, or an object that makes the sound? Almost always, the answer will be one of those two — and the context will make it perfectly clear which one.
